statements.text: The CCP has invested heavily in artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies.
statements.context: Opening statement by Rep. Gus Bilirakis, chair of the Innovation, Data, and Commerce Subcommittee, at a hearing on US-China economic competition.

statements.text: I would like to start with Ms. Espinel. [...] Can you tell me how conducting impact assessments and calculating risks will serve us well in data privacy legislation and prevent harms in AI.
statements.context: House Energy & Commerce subcommittee hearing on AI and data privacy, chaired by Mr. Bilirakis, with full committee chairman Mrs. Rodgers questioning a witness.

statements.text: despite years of trying, we have no foundation for how consumer data is collected, used, and properly secured. We need to get the fundamentals in place. [...] Can you expand on that and speak to how important it is for us to have a preemptive national standard to ensure data privacy and security for our constituents and for American leadership on AI.
statements.context: House committee hearing titled 'Safeguarding Data and Innovation: Building the Foundation for the Use of Artificial Intelligence.'

statements.text: Without a data privacy and security standard that dictates the rules for how companies can collect, process, store, and transfer information, bad actors may have unfettered access to use and exploit our most sensitive information.
statements.context: Opening statement by Rep. Bilirakis, chair of the House Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Innovation, Data, and Commerce, at a hearing on AI and data privacy.

statements.text: We know these large AI systems harvest and scrape the internet for data, and that includes personal information due to the data breaches and hacking, amongst other causes. This can be used for deepfakes and other scams that I will call digitized fraud.
statements.context: Rep. Bilirakis questioning a witness at a House Energy & Commerce Subcommittee hearing on AI and data innovation.

statements.text: What recommendations do you have for the healthcare sector to leverage artificial importance, privacy enhancing technologies, and other best practices to better protect against new threats as they appear?
statements.context: House Energy & Commerce Subcommittee on Innovation, Data, and Commerce hearing on health sector cybersecurity after the Change Healthcare ransomware attack.

statements.text: Mr. Speaker, I move to suspend the rules and pass the bill (H.R. 4814) to direct the Consumer Product Safety Commission to establish a pilot program to explore the use of artificial intelligence in support of the mission of the Commission [...] Not later than 1 year after the date of the enactment of this Act, the Consumer Product Safety Commission shall establish a pilot program to explore the use of artificial intelligence by the Commission in support of the consumer product safety mission of the Commission [...]
statements.context: House floor debate on suspending the rules to pass H.R. 4814, the Consumer Safety Technology Act.

statements.text: It should be no surprise, Mr. Speaker, that the global race for economic dominance today is centered around technology, specifically around emerging technologies like artificial intelligence and blockchain.
statements.context: Floor statement in the U.S. House of Representatives in support of H.R. 4814, the Consumer Safety Technology Act.

statements.text: But I think we must remember that generative AI is only a specific use case of this technology, and AI’s applications are much broader than what has claimed the spotlight recently. We have seen how AI applied to vehicles is paving the way for the next generation of vehicles that will drive themselves.
statements.venue: Opening statement, House E&C CMT Subcommittee hearing on American leadership in manufacturing

statements.text: So AI, I think what we have to make sure is that AI, which will certainly increase the volume of work that we do, that we are able to bring about in manufacturing, but what I am concerned about is that ordinary workers are also going to be considered when we talk about AI, and that they are not going to be—because there is going to be a lot more manufacturing that is done with AI, but what is going to happen to everyday Americans? So I think that has to be part of the consideration.
statements.context: Remarks by Rep. Jan Schakowsky at a House Energy and Commerce subcommittee hearing on AI in manufacturing.

statements.text: AI has already enveloped itself into the manufacturing ecosystem, and it is creating more efficient systems to build here in America. We need to do more to encourage this type of growth here at home.
statements.context: House subcommittee hearing on AI in manufacturing, during the questioning portion led by Rep. Bilirakis.

statements.text: We know generative AI is currently dominating the headlines for its specific use case of AI, such as how DeepSeek is capturing warranted attention with their collection of Americans' personal data and subsequently sharing it with the Chinese Communist Party. But I think we must remember that generative AI—and, of course, you know, has some positive aspects, there is no question. [...] We have also seen how the technology holds the power to completely revolutionize American manufacturing and bolster our supply chain. By integrating AI and machine learning into supply chain systems, we can better predict constraints and find potential weak points, which can be used to prevent shocks that disrupt entire industries.
statements.context: Opening statement by Rep. Gus Bilirakis, chair of the Commerce, Manufacturing, and Trade Subcommittee, at a hearing on AI in manufacturing.

statements.text: A teacher in my district used AI to create explicit content of his students incorporating real images of his students taken from a yearbook.
statements.context: House floor speech in support of S. 146, the TAKE IT DOWN Act, during legislative debate.

statements.text: Mr. Speaker, I move to suspend the rules and pass the bill (S. 146) to require covered platforms to remove nonconsensual intimate visual depictions, and for other purposes. [...] The term `digital forgery' means any intimate visual depiction of an identifiable individual created through the use of software, machine learning, artificial intelligence, or any other computer-generated or technological means, including by adapting, modifying, manipulating, or altering an authentic visual depiction, that, when viewed as a whole by a reasonable person, is indistinguishable from an authentic visual depiction of the individual.
statements.context: House floor motion by Rep. Bilirakis to suspend the rules and pass S. 146, the TAKE IT DOWN Act, which criminalizes nonconsensual intimate deepfakes and requires platform removal.

statements.text: Mr. Bhargava, you have stated that the VC firms like General Catalyst as well as AI startups are already starting to address potential risks around AI. Can you share more about what these steps look like and how government can work with, rather than against, AI innovators to support AI innovation and protect consumers, please?
statements.context: Exchange during a congressional hearing on AI regulation and U.S. leadership.

statements.text: Like every technology, however, AI can be weaponized when it is in the wrong hands. Thankfully, AI is already regulated by longstanding laws that protect consumers.
statements.context: Opening remarks by Chairman Bilirakis at a House Energy & Commerce Subcommittee on Innovation hearing on AI regulation and U.S. leadership.

statements.text: Like every technology, however, AI can be weaponized when it is in the wrong hands, as you know. [...] Because of the great potential of these technologies, Congress must be careful when we impose additional obligations on AI developers and deployers.
statements.context: Opening statement by Rep. Gus Bilirakis at a House Energy and Commerce subcommittee hearing on AI regulation and U.S. leadership.

statements.text: Beyond the law, the EU also establishes a code of practice. While not currently mandatory, we are concerned that it will function as a de facto benchmark for evaluating industry compliance with the law. The code mandates extensive disclosure of sensitive business information to the regulator, downstream providers, competitors including China, and potentially the public. This raises two major risks: First, releasing the know-how behind the technology could enable misuse of powerful AI systems; and, second, forcing the value of IP being disclosed undermines investment incentives.
statements.context: House Energy and Commerce subcommittee hearing on AI regulation and U.S. leadership, featuring private-sector testimony from the U.S. Chamber of Commerce.

statements.text: And the answer is not zero, but the answer is not — the AI, I understand it takes 330,000 euro, that is probably about $350,000, just to comply with one of the act's requirements.
statements.context: House Energy and Commerce Committee hearing on AI regulation, with a member yielding time to the full committee chairman who discusses AI competition and regulatory structure.

statements.text: And should we be concerned that the AI Act will be used for similar ends?
statements.context: House hearing titled 'AI Regulation and the Future of US Leadership,' with the chair questioning a witness about transatlantic regulatory enforcement.

statements.text: Thankfully, AI is already regulated by longstanding laws that protect consumers. Because of the great potential of these technologies, Congress must be careful when we impose additional obligations on AI developers and deployers.
statements.venue: Opening statement, House E&C Commerce, Manufacturing, and Trade Subcommittee hearing on AI regulation

statements.text: Our task is to protect our citizens and ensure that we don’t cede U.S. AI leadership. [...] And heavy-handed regulations may ensure that the next great American company never makes it. If we fail in this task, we risk ceding American leadership in AI to China, which is close on our heels.
statements.venue: Opening statement, House E&C Commerce, Manufacturing, and Trade Subcommittee hearing on AI regulation

statements.text: The E.U. recently enacted its own 'AI Act.' While it is still being implemented, the E.U.’s complex law suffers from many of the innovation-chilling effects we saw with the GDPR.
statements.venue: Opening statement, House E&C Commerce, Manufacturing, and Trade Subcommittee hearing on AI regulation

statements.text: Can you talk more about how AI is being used or can be used to prevent human rights abuses, war crimes, and other acts of persecution?
statements.context: House subcommittee hearing on AI applications in communications and technology, featuring a member's question to a witness about AI's potential to counter persecution.

statements.text: So, Mr. Pickering, how can AI be used, utilized, to actually track down online and by-phone criminals that are preying on our seniors in particular and finally shut them down once and for all?
statements.context: Congressman Bilirakis questioning a witness at a House Energy and Commerce subcommittee hearing on AI applications in communications and technology.

statements.text: Dr. Fontes, looking forward to the future, we must. [...] How do you envision AI being utilized to enhance emergency response in the future, and how can Congress help to make that the reality?
statements.context: Rep. Bilirakis questions a witness during a congressional hearing on public safety communications.

statements.text: We heard stories of chatbots encouraging and facilitating suicides in kids. The KIDS Act, sponsored by the Chairman, addresses that.
statements.venue: Remarks at House Energy and Commerce Committee markup of the KIDS Act, as reported by Florida Politics

statements.text: AI is the leading use case for semiconductors, and the AI surge is responsible for over half of total semiconductor revenue – potentially reaching 500 billion dollars this year, and 1 trillion dollars by 2030.
statements.context: Opening statement by Rep. Gus Bilirakis, Chairman of the Commerce, Manufacturing, and Trade Subcommittee, at a hearing on the semiconductor ecosystem and AI-driven demand.

statements.text: Between congressional and executive action, including actions in this committee, there has been an array of actions to strengthen U.S. global semiconductor leadership.
statements.context: Opening statement by Rep. Bilirakis at a House Energy and Commerce subcommittee hearing on the semiconductor ecosystem and U.S.-China strategic competition.

statements.text: Agreed. To win the race against China, American AI companies need to succeed at home and abroad. However, we have seen foreign trading partners, especially the EU, enact sweeping new AI data regulations that could be used to target U.S. companies. Mr. Mahmood, how can we address new and emerging digital trade barriers to ensure American AI companies can outcompete their Chinese competitors on an even playing field?
statements.context: U.S. House hearing titled 'China's Campaign to Steal America's AI Edge,' where Representative Bilirakis questions a witness about digital trade barriers facing U.S. AI firms.

statements.text: The rise of artificial intelligence presents incredible opportunities, but innovation must never come at the expense of those who create original content. News organizations invest significant time and resources to produce accurate, reliable journalism that keeps our communities informed. It is simply wrong for AI bots to scrape that content, repurpose it, and profit from it without permission or compensation,
statements.venue: Press release on introducing the Stealth Bot Prohibition Act
